Lyse
LEE-seh
n. (the Norwegian Cistercian abbey of 1146 near Bergen, the first of the order in Norway, settled from Fountains)
Norwegian Lyse, from the Lysefjord; latinised Lysa.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lyse south of Bergen was founded in 1146 by Bishop Sigurd of Bergen and settled from Fountains in Yorkshire, the first Cistercian house in Norway and the mother of Tautra and of Hovedoya. Monks came north by sea from an English dale to a Norwegian fjord, cleared and farmed, and the house held estates along the western coast until the Reformation dissolved it in 1537. Little stands. The dictionary records Lyse for the direction of travel, which is the ordinary pattern of Christian expansion: men sent from a settled place to an unsettled one. The Lord's own statement of the problem is a shortage of workers rather than of ground, “The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37), and He forbids the delay that always sounds prudent, “Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest” (Joh 4:35). The sowing is expected to cost those who do it, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5), and the charge over whatever congregation results is given in terms of its price, “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a mission as a sending, also a station of missionaries; a fjord would be an inlet of the sea; to colonize as to plant a colony; a daughter-house is a convent founded from another; and harvest as the season of reaping.

expand to see more

MISSION, n. A sending or being sent, usually by authority, on some business; persons sent; a station of missionaries.

FIRTH, n. A narrow arm or inlet of the sea; an estuary; the opening of a river into the sea.

COLONIZE, v.t. To plant or establish a colony in; to plant or settle a number of the subjects of a kingdom in a remote country.

FILIATION, n. The relation of a son to a father; also, the relation of a dependent house to its parent.

HARVEST, n. The season of reaping and gathering grain or other crops; the ripe corn or grain collected.

Key Scripture

Mat 9:37 — "Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;"

Joh 4:35 — "Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest? behold, I say unto you, Lift up your eyes, and look on the fields; for they are white already to harvest."

Psa 126:5 — "They that sow in tears shall reap in joy."

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

Modern Corruption

Norway's first Cistercian house, 1146, settled from Fountains in Yorkshire, mother of Tautra and Hovedoya.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that expansion is men sent, not territory acquired. Lyse was planted by Yorkshire monks who went north by sea, and the Lord's own account of what is scarce in such work is not land, “but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37).

The live temptation is to count estates instead of converts, which is what the Norwegian houses eventually did. Christ refuses the postponement that makes such counting restful, “Say not ye, There are yet four months, and then cometh harvest?” (Joh 4:35); the sowing is expected to be costly, “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5); and the flock that results is valued by what it cost its owner, “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek therismos (G2326), a harvest; Greek ergates (G2040), a workman; Hebrew zara (H2232), to sow; Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer.

expand to see more

Greek therismos (G2326) — a harvest, a reaping; “The harvest truly is plenteous”, Matthew 9:37.

Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, a labourer; “but the labourers are few”, Matthew 9:37.

Greek leukos (G3022) — white, bright; “they are white already to harvest”, John 4:35.

Hebrew zara (H2232) — to sow, to scatter seed; “They that sow in tears”, Psalm 126:5.

Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend, to shepherd; “to feed the church of God”, Acts 20:28.

Usage

"“but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — what is actually scarce."

"“they are white already to harvest” (Joh 4:35) — the prudent delay refused."

"“which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28) — what a flock cost."
